messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 29
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: Middle Eastern
- Relationship Status: Single
- Occupation: Train Conductor
- Trauma Type: Witnessed other trauma
- Pcl5: 43

He is a 29-year-old Middle Eastern man who works as a train conductor and lives alone, keeping his life tightly organized around work, sleep, and the commute between. Before the event, he describes himself as steady, practical, and not especially emotional. He takes pride in being the kind of person who knows the routes, notices problems early, and can stay calm when other people panic.

About a year ago, while working a late evening shift, he witnesses a fatal accident on the platform of a crowded station. A person steps too close to the edge and falls into the path of an oncoming train. He remembers the sound more than anything at first: the scream of brakes, the sharp metal impact, and then the terrible silence that follows. He does not see everything clearly, but he sees enough to know that it is serious. In the moment, he moves automatically, shouting for people to back away, trying to keep the crowd from flooding the area, and then helping direct emergency responders when they arrive. He stays on site longer than his shift requires, partly because no one tells him to leave and partly because he cannot seem to make himself go home.

In the days afterward, he finds himself replaying the scene in fragments. At work, he is able to function, but only by forcing himself into a narrow, rigid focus. He checks the platform repeatedly, counts passengers twice, and watches the tracks with a vigilance that borders on scanning. He says that after the accident he begins to feel as if danger can appear anywhere, at any time, and that he is the only one who might notice it in time. He becomes more irritable with coworkers, especially when they joke about delays or complain about minor problems. He hears himself snapping and then feels ashamed, but he cannot seem to soften.

Sleep becomes difficult. He lies in bed listening for sounds from the street below, and when he does drift off, he wakes suddenly with his heart racing, certain for a moment that he has heard the brakes again. Some nights he dreams not of the event itself but of being unable to move while people call out for help. He wakes sweaty and disoriented, then sits in the dark for a long time before he can calm himself enough to try again. On workdays he drinks more coffee than he used to, telling himself it helps him stay alert, though it leaves him jittery and unable to relax even when he gets home.

He avoids the platform where the accident happened whenever possible, and if his route requires him to pass through that station, he feels his body tense before he even arrives. He notices his chest tighten, his hands becoming damp, and his thoughts narrowing to one idea: get through it, don’t look, keep moving. He begins choosing different cars on the train when he commutes as a passenger, preferring to stand near exits. He no longer likes crowded places and has stopped meeting friends for drinks after work. The small circle he keeps is mostly coworkers and one cousin he speaks with by phone, though even those conversations feel effortful. He says people ask how he is doing, and he gives the same answer every time because the truth feels hard to explain.

He carries a persistent sense of guilt, even though he knows he did not cause the accident. He wonders whether he could have noticed something sooner, whether he should have done more, whether he failed the person who died by not being faster or more certain. He returns to these thoughts when he is alone, especially at night, and he finds that the more he tries to push them away, the more sharply they come back. At times he feels detached from his own life, as if he is moving through routines that belong to someone else. He goes to work, eats what is in the refrigerator, and answers messages, but he does these things with a sense of effort, as though each task requires more energy than it should.

Over time, he notices that ordinary noises can pull him back into the memory: the screech of a train wheel, a sudden shout, even the jolt of a stopped car at a crossing. His body reacts before his mind can catch up. He startsle easily, looks over his shoulder often, and sits with his back to the wall in restaurants. He says he is tired in a way sleep does not fix. Still, he keeps showing up, putting on his uniform, checking the schedule, and stepping onto the train each day with a face he has learned to keep composed.
